title: 6 · Storage, File Organisation & Indexing (Unit 4)
learn:
Storage hierarchy

Media differ in speed, cost and reliability. Primary: cache and main memory (fastest, most expensive, volatile). Secondary: flash and magnetic disk (non-volatile; flash reads fast but writes/erases slowly). Tertiary: optical disk and magnetic tape, used mainly for backups. Going down, cost falls and access time rises.

File organisation

A database is a collection of files; a file is a sequence of records; a record is a sequence of fields. Data moves between disk and RAM in whole blocks. Records per block = block size ÷ record size (512 B ÷ 4 B = 128 records).

Spanned: a record may be split across blocks (no wasted space but reading one record may need two blocks). Unspanned: a record always sits in one block (block 10 B, record 3 B: 3 records fit and 1 B is wasted). Most databases use unspanned. Records can be unordered (fast insert, slow search) or ordered on an attribute.

Indexing

An index reduces disk accesses. Each entry has a search key and a data reference (pointer) to a disk block. Dense: an entry for every search-key value. Sparse: entries for only some records. Example: SK 1→B1 (records 1-10), 11→B2, 21→B3, 31→B4; to find record 25, go straight to block 3.

Single-level: primary (ordered file, key), clustering (ordered file, non-key), secondary (unordered file). Multilevel: B-tree and B+-tree.

lab.task: Block 1024 B, record 100 B. Unspanned: records per block and wasted bytes? Spanned: how many blocks for 1000 records?
lab.solution: Unspanned: floor(1024/100)=10 records, 24 B wasted. Spanned: 1000×100 = 100,000 B ÷ 1024 = 97.66, so 98 blocks.
